summary: This Standards Track document specifies a Non-Queue-Building Per-Hop Behavior for Differentiated Services. It gives a shallow-buffered best-effort service next to the default deep-buffered one, so smooth, low-rate, application-limited flows avoid the delay and loss that queue-building traffic causes. It updates RFC 8325.

plainLanguage.summary: On a busy access link, a deep queue forms because the sending algorithms push more data into the link than it can carry. Everything sharing the link then waits longer, including short messages that are sensitive to delay and did nothing to cause the queue. This document defines a way for such traffic to be marked and given a small queue of its own, so that it is not held up behind the bulk traffic.

questions: what dscp is used for nqb
what is a non queue building flow
subtitle: A separate shallow-buffered queue, marked with DSCP 45, so small smooth flows avoid the delay caused by big capacity-seeking ones.

tldr.problem: Most access links use a congestion control algorithm that overshoots the available capacity, so a deep queue builds up and every flow sharing that link sees extra delay and loss. Small flows such as voice calls and DNS lookups suffer most, even though they contribute almost nothing to the queue.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9956 defines a Non-Queue-Building per-hop behavior. Senders that keep their rate near 1% of the path capacity and pace their packets mark their traffic with DSCP 45, and nodes give that traffic a queue of its own with a buffer of 10 ms or less, scheduled equally with the Default queue.
tldr.outcome: The document registers DSCP 45 for the behavior and sets the rules for the node, including a traffic protection function that detects traffic marked as NQB that does not behave that way and either reclassifies or discards it. It updates RFC 8325 and is designed for broadband access links.

facts.label: Maximum sender rate
facts.value: About 1% of the typical network path capacity

facts.label: Pacing rule
facts.value: Bytes sent in any interval T are at most (R * T) + MTU

facts.label: Recommended NQB buffer
facts.value: 10 ms or less at the shared NQB and Default egress rate

today: RFC 9956 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2026, and it has not been obsoleted. IANA has assigned DSCP 45 for NQB behaviour from the DSCP Pool 3 codepoints, and the document updates RFC 8325. The behaviour is designed for broadband access links, where the buffer is deep and traffic is not heavily aggregated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document defines a Diffserv per-hop behavior called the Non-Queue-Building Per-Hop Behavior. The NQB PHB isolates traffic microflows, that is application-to-application flows, that have relatively low data rates and that do not themselves materially contribute to queuing delay and loss. This isolation allows those microflows to avoid the queuing delay and losses caused by other traffic.

Microflows such as interactive voice, game sync packets, certain machine-to-machine applications, DNS lookups and some real-time Internet of Things analytics data are low-data-rate, application-limited microflows. They can be distinguished from bursty traffic microflows and high-data-rate microflows managed by a classic congestion control algorithm, both of which cause queuing delay and loss.

In accordance with IETF guidance, most packets carried by access networks are managed by an end-to-end congestion control algorithm. Many of the commonly deployed algorithms, such as Reno, CUBIC or BBR, are designed to seek the available capacity of the path from sender to receiver, which can frequently be the access network link capacity. In doing so they generally overshoot the available capacity, causing a queue to build up at the bottleneck link. That queue buildup results in variable delay and packet loss that can affect all the applications sharing the bottleneck link. Moreover, many bottleneck links implement a relatively deep buffer, of 100 ms or more, in order to let these congestion control algorithms use the link efficiently, which exacerbates the delay and delay variation experienced.

In contrast to applications that frequently cause queuing delay, there are a variety of relatively low data rate applications that do not materially contribute to it, yet are subjected to it by sharing the same bottleneck link. Many of these applications are sensitive to delay or delay variation as well as to packet loss, so they produce a poor quality of experience in such conditions.

Active queue management mechanisms intended for single queues can improve the experience for delay-sensitive applications, but there are practical limits to how much improvement can be achieved without impacting the throughput of capacity-seeking applications. Flow-queuing systems can isolate microflows from one another, but they are not appropriate for all bottleneck links, because of reasons that include complexity.

The NQB PHB supports differentiating between the two classes of traffic in bottleneck links and queuing them separately, so that both classes deliver a satisfactory experience. It provides a shallow-buffered, best-effort service as a complement to the Default deep-buffered, best-effort service, and is designed for broadband access network links, where there is minimal aggregation of traffic and buffers are deep. A network implementing the NQB PHB solely provides isolation for traffic classified as behaving in conformance with the described behaviors; a node supporting the PHB makes no guarantees on delay or data rate for NQB-marked microflows beyond the delay bound provided by the shallow buffer. It is the senders' own behaviour that results in low delay and low loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The document separates two kinds of traffic. One kind fills the link and builds a queue; the other kind is small, steady and would never fill it on its own. The second kind is still hurt by the queue the first kind builds, because they share one buffer. Giving the second kind its own small buffer is the whole idea.

sections.title: Queue-Building and Non-Queue-Building Traffic
sections.content:
There are applications that send traffic at relatively low data rates, or in a fairly smooth and consistent manner, such that they are unlikely to exceed the available capacity of the network path between sender and receiver even at an inter-packet timescale. Some of these applications are transactional in nature and might only send one packet, or a few packets, per round-trip time. These applications might cause only very small transient queues to form in network buffers; nonetheless they can be subjected to delay and delay variation as a result of sharing a network buffer with applications that tend to cause large or standing queues. These applications typically respond to network congestion by discontinuing, or significantly reducing, their transmissions, and they can be negatively affected by excessive delay and delay variation. Such applications are ideal candidates to be queued separately from the applications that cause the queue buildup.

In contrast, QB microflows include those that probe for link capacity and induce delay and loss as a result, for example microflows that use CUBIC, Reno or other TCP and QUIC congestion control algorithms in a capacity-seeking manner. Other types of QB microflows send at a high burst rate even if the long-term average data rate is much lower.
sections.plainLanguage: A non-queue-building flow is one that asks for little and asks evenly. A queue-building flow is one that keeps pushing to find out how much the link will take, or that sends in bursts. The first kind would hardly notice the link on its own, and the second kind is the reason the link is busy.

sections.title: Relationship to L4S and Applicability
sections.content:
The NQB DSCP and PHB are defined to operate independently of the Low Latency, Low Loss and Scalable throughput architecture. Traffic marked with the NQB DSCP is nevertheless intended to be compatible with L4S, with the result that NQB traffic and L4S traffic can share the low-latency queue in an L4S DualQ node. A network node's compliance with the DualQ Coupled AQM requirements is considered sufficient to support the NQB PHB requirement of fair allocation of capacity between the QB and NQB queues, and those requirements in turn require compliance with all the requirements of RFC 9331.

Applications that comply with both the NQB sender requirements and the Prague L4S requirements could mark their packets both with the NQB DSCP and with the ECT(1) value. In nodes that support both the NQB PHB and L4S, the L4S network functions should treat packets marked with the NQB DSCP and ECT(1) or Congestion Experienced the same as packets marked with the Default DSCP and the same Explicit Congestion Notification value.

This PHB is primarily applicable for high-speed broadband access network links, where there is minimal aggregation of traffic and deep buffers are common. In many other links, forwarding NQB-marked packets using the Default treatment might be sufficient to preserve the loss, delay and delay-variation performance for NQB traffic. This is generally true in links that do not typically experience congestion, such as many backbone and core network links, and in highly aggregated links designed to carry a large number of simultaneous microflows, where individual microflow burstiness is averaged out and is therefore unlikely to cause much actual delay.
sections.plainLanguage: The behaviour is designed for the access link, where one household's traffic is not mixed with hundreds of others and the buffer is deep. On a backbone link that is rarely busy, or on a link carrying so many flows that their bursts average out, the extra queue would buy little. The document also says how the marking behaves alongside the L4S low-latency architecture, so that the two can share one queue.

sections.title: Sender Requirements
sections.content:
Microflows that are eligible to be marked with the NQB DSCP send non-bursty traffic at a low data rate relative to typical network path capacities. The data rate is limited by the application itself rather than by network capacity: these microflows send at a data rate of no more than about 1% of the typical network path capacity. In addition they are required to be sent in a smooth, that is paced, manner, where the number of IP bytes sent in any time interval T is less than or equal to (R * T) + MTU, where R is the maximum rate described above, expressed in bytes per second. For example, at the time of writing access network data rates are typically on the order of 50 Mbps or more, which implies 500 kbps as an upper limit. Microflows are unidirectional, while application traffic is often bidirectional, so for a particular application some of its microflows may be eligible to be marked while others are not: an interactive video streaming application might consist of a high-bandwidth video stream that is not eligible in one direction and a low-bandwidth control stream that is eligible in the other.

Microflows marked with the NQB DSCP are expected to comply with existing guidance for safe deployment on the Internet, including the guidance related to response to network congestion. The fact that a microflow's data rate is low relative to typical network capacities is no guarantee that sufficient capacity exists in any particular network, and it is the responsibility of the application to detect and react appropriately if the network capacity is insufficient.

Applications are recommended to use the DSCP value 45 to mark microflows as NQB. The choice is motivated in part by the desire to achieve separate queuing in existing Wi-Fi networks, and by the desire to make the implementation of the PHB simpler in equipment that can classify traffic based on ranges of DSCP values. The two primary considerations for whether an application chooses to mark its traffic as NQB involve the risk of being subjected to a traffic protection algorithm, and the consequences of overrunning the NQB shallow buffer. To avoid these risks, if a microflow's traffic exceeds the rate equation, the application must not mark that traffic with the NQB DSCP.

All the sender requirements relate to observable attributes of the packet stream, which makes it possible for network elements to monitor for inappropriate usage of the DSCP and take action on traffic that does not comply.
sections.plainLanguage: An application may mark its traffic only if it keeps to two rules. Its rate must be no more than about 1% of the path capacity, and it must send evenly, so that the number of bytes sent in any interval T never exceeds R times T plus one packet's worth. The marking is DSCP 45. If the application breaks the rules, it must stop using that marking, because the network will act on it.

sections.title: Per-Hop Behavior Requirements
sections.content:
A node supporting the NQB PHB must provide a queue for NQB traffic separate from the queue used for Default traffic, and should not rate limit or police the aggregate of NQB traffic separately from Default traffic. The NQB queue should be given equivalent forwarding preference compared to the Default queue, and the node should provide a scheduler that allows NQB and Default traffic to share the link in a manner that treats the two classes equally, for example a Deficit Round-Robin scheduler with equal weights, or two Wireless Multimedia Access Categories with the same Enhanced Distributed Channel Access parameters. A node that provides rate limits or guarantees for Default traffic should ensure that such limits and guarantees are shared with NQB traffic in a manner that treats the two classes equally.

Ideally the scheduler weight would match the highest fraction of capacity that compliant flows are likely to use on a particular network segment. Since compliant flows are not capacity seeking, and since DRR allows unused capacity in one class to be used by traffic in the other, a higher-than-needed NQB weight is less problematic than the reverse. It does, however, increase the likelihood that a non-compliant microflow mis-marked as NQB is able to use more than its fair share. NQB microflows are expected to consume no more than 1% of the link capacity each, and in low statistical multiplexing environments, such as at the edge of the network, would be unlikely in aggregate to consume 50% of the link capacity, so 50% seems a reasonable upper bound on the weight for the NQB PHB in these environments.

By default, a node supporting the NQB PHB should classify packets marked with DSCP 45 into the NQB queue, and must support the ability to configure the DSCP used for that classification. It may support the ability to configure multiple DSCPs for it.

Support for the NQB PHB is advantageous at bottleneck nodes. Many bottleneck nodes have a relatively deep buffer for Default traffic, roughly equal to the base round-trip time of the expected connections, which could be tens or hundreds of milliseconds. Providing a similarly deep buffer for the NQB queue would be at cross purposes to providing very low queuing delay. The NQB queue must have a buffer size that is significantly smaller than the buffer provided for Default traffic, and it is recommended to configure an NQB buffer size of 10 ms or less at the shared NQB and Default egress rate.

In order to enable network operators to monitor the usage of the PHB and to monitor for potential mis-marking, a node supporting the NQB PHB must provide statistics that can be used to detect whether abuse is occurring, for example packet and drop counters.
sections.plainLanguage: At the bottleneck, the traffic gets its own queue, and that queue is deliberately small: 10 ms or less, where the Default queue might hold 100 ms or more of traffic. The two queues are scheduled evenly, so neither gets preference. And the node has to count what it drops, so that an operator can see whether the queue is overflowing and whose traffic is causing it.

sections.title: Traffic Protection
sections.content:
It is possible that, because of an implementation error or misconfiguration, a QB microflow could end up being mis-marked as NQB or vice versa. It is also possible that a malicious actor could introduce a QB microflow marked as NQB with the intention of causing disruptions. A QB microflow mis-marked as NQB is able to contribute to NQB queue formation at a network node, which would cause queuing delay or loss for all the other microflows sharing the NQB queue.

To prevent this, network elements that support the NQB PHB should support a traffic protection function that can identify microflows or packets inconsistent with the sender requirements and either reclassify them to the QB queue or discard the offending traffic. A reclassifying implementation may offer the option of additionally re-marking such traffic to Default, or to another local codepoint, so that the result of the decision can be used by further hops. This sort of re-marking could provide a limited layer of protection where downstream nodes support separate queuing for NQB-marked packets but lack traffic protection.

If traffic protection is not supported or is not effective, mis-marked QB traffic is able to form a queue that overflows the shallow buffer, which is expected to result in redirecting the excess packets to the QB queue or discarding them. Both actions degrade service for the mis-marked traffic and for the correctly marked NQB traffic. An implementation that does not support traffic protection therefore risks being limited to deployments where it is not needed, such as a controlled enterprise network where an administrator manages the use of the DSCP values.

Traffic protection as defined here differs from traffic conditioning in other Diffserv contexts, which is commonly performed at the edge of a domain. Traffic protection is intended to be implemented in the nodes that implement the PHB, so that an implementation can monitor the actual NQB queue and take action only if a queue begins to form. The specification does not mandate a particular algorithm, since this is probably an area where implementers will innovate. The traffic protection function should not base its decisions on application-layer constructs such as the port number or the source and destination address, but on the actual behaviour of each microflow, that is the pattern of packet arrivals.

A conventional implementation is a per-microflow rate policer that identifies microflows exceeding the bound set out in the sender requirements, with R set to 1% of the egress link capacity available for NQB traffic. An alternative bases decisions on the detection of actual queuing, by monitoring the queuing delay experienced by packets in the NQB queue in correlation with the arrival of packets for each microflow. A per-microflow rate policer is conceptually simpler and is based directly on the sender requirements, but it can end up more strict than necessary, for example by policing a flow that exceeds the rate equation even when the link is underutilized.

Where the algorithm reclassifies offending traffic, different levels of hysteresis could be considered, for example deciding packet by packet, which could result in significant out-of-order delivery, or employing enough hysteresis to prevent borderline microflows from being reclassified capriciously. Where the algorithm discards offending traffic, it is recommended that the decision thresholds be set higher than in designs that reclassify, since discarding a packet is likely to cause more degradation than out-of-order delivery. The function must be designed so that the node does not fail, for example by crashing, in the case where the microflow state is exhausted.

Some networks might prefer to police the application of the NQB DSCP at the ingress edge instead, using a per-microflow rate policer at 1% of the minimum link capacity of the network. That approach is generally expected to be inferior, because an edge node cannot guarantee that there would never be more than 100 NQB flows sharing a single internal bottleneck, and there could be internal links with much greater capacity than the minimum. Traffic conditioning at the edge could therefore be simultaneously too lenient and too strict.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk is that a bulk transfer lies and gets marked as though it were a small, steady flow. It would then fill the small queue and slow down everyone who really is a small, steady flow. The document therefore asks nodes to watch for traffic marked as NQB that does not behave that way, and either put it back in the ordinary queue or drop it. The check should be based on how the packets arrive, not on the port number or address, so that the decision cannot be faked.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The document gives guidance for network operators on the identification, marking and handling of NQB traffic, on aggregation behaviours, and on special considerations in unmanaged and inter-network scenarios.

Nodes supporting the PHB provide for the configuration of classifiers that can differentiate between QB and NQB traffic of equivalent importance, and the assigned NQB DSCP value of 45 is recommended as the default classifier to distinguish NQB traffic from traffic classified as Default, which has DSCP 0.

It is recommended that networks and nodes that do not support the NQB PHB be configured to treat traffic marked with the NQB DSCP the same as traffic with the Default DSCP. This includes networks such as MPLS and nodes that aggregate service classes, where the recommendation results in traffic marked with the NQB DSCP being aggregated into the Elastic Treatment Aggregate or the Default and Elastic Treatment Aggregate. Such networks and nodes ought to classify packets with the NQB DSCP value into the appropriate treatment aggregate, or encapsulate them for purposes of aggregation, and should not re-mark them with a different DSCP. Preserving the NQB DSCP value enables hops further along the path to provide the NQB PHB successfully.

The document also covers the aggregation of other DSCPs into the NQB PHB, cross-domain usage and DSCP re-marking, the behaviour of the NQB DSCP with tunnels, and guidance for lower-rate links.
sections.plainLanguage: A node that does not implement this behaviour should still carry the marked traffic in its ordinary queue and must not change the marking, because a later node on the path might implement the behaviour and the marking is what tells it to. Re-marking the traffic would throw that away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations for the NQB PHB relate to the potential to impact the capacity available, or the delay experienced, by other flows that share a bottleneck with traffic marked with the recommended NQB DSCP.

Full support for the PHB in bottleneck links limits the incentives for a QB application to mis-mark its packets as NQB, particularly for implementations that support traffic protection. If a QB microflow were to mis-mark its packets as NQB it would be unlikely to receive a benefit, and it would usually experience a degradation, in contrast to mis-marking packets for a higher-priority behaviour such as the Expedited Forwarding PHB. The nature of the degradation depends on the specifics of the implementation, including the response to NQB buffer overflow and the presence or absence of a traffic protection function, and could include excessive packet loss, excessive delay variation, or excessive out-of-order delivery. If an NQB microflow were to fail to mark its packets as NQB, it could suffer the delay and loss typical of sharing a queue with capacity-seeking traffic.

To preserve low-delay performance for NQB traffic, networks that support the PHB will need to ensure that mechanisms are in place to prevent malicious traffic marked with the NQB DSCP from causing excessive queue delay. The recommendations presume that some type of flow state is maintained, to differentiate between microflows that cause queuing delay and those that do not. Since that state is likely finite, this opens the possibility of flow-state exhaustion attacks, and the traffic protection mechanism must be designed with that possibility in mind.

If traffic protection is not implemented, or is unable to prevent queue formation, the limited size of the shallow buffer means a growing queue overruns it, resulting in negative effects such as reforwarding as Default or discarding that can affect multiple NQB-marked microflows, independent of whether each contributed to the queue formation. Those effects discourage misuse by QB traffic, but their effect on the NQB traffic that is using the buffer as intended motivates limiting the effects of shallow buffer overrun through per-user provisioning limits.
sections.plainLanguage: The risk here is not that someone reads a message; it is that someone floods the small queue and ruins the service for everyone who marked their traffic correctly. The document expects nodes to detect that, and it notes that the state needed to detect it is finite, so a node has to be designed to survive having that state used up.
